entry: War between [[Russia]] and Chechen separatists, August 1999–April 2009, fought in [[Chechnya]] and the border regions of the North Caucasus. Islamists from Chechnya infiltrated [[Dagestan]] in August 1999, and apartment bombings in Russian cities later that year killed over 300 people. Russian authorities blamed Chechens, though no Chechen group claimed responsibility. Russian forces seized Grozny after a winter siege (December 1999–February 2000) and established direct rule in May 2000. The military phase ended in April 2002, and by 2009 Russia had disabled the separatist movement. Both sides attacked civilians. Total deaths, including combatants and non-combatants, are estimated at over 60,000.

Christian and Islamic belief that [[Jesus]] will return to Earth after his Ascension to Heaven. Also called the Second Advent or the *parousia*, the idea rests on messianic prophecies and is part of most Christian [[Eschatology|eschatologies]]. The Greek word *parousia* means "arrival," "coming" or "presence," and the [[New Testament]] uses it 24 times, seventeen of them concerning Christ. In Islamic eschatology, Jesus (*ʿĪsā ibn Maryam*) is also expected to return at the end times, defeating the false messiah (*al-Masih ad-Dajjal*), restoring justice and reaffirming monotheism. Islam regards him as a revered prophet rather than as divine, and his return is a major sign of the Day of Judgment. Some minor religious movements have held that their founder was a later incarnation of Jesus Christ. A 2010 survey found that about 40% of Americans believed Jesus was likely to return by 2050.

War centered on the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]] (DRC) from 1998 to 2003, also known as Africa's World War. It began on August 2, 1998, when President Laurent-Désiré Kabila turned against his former allies from [[Rwanda]] and [[Uganda]], who had helped him seize power. The war drew in nine African nations and about 25 armed groups. Rwandan and rebel forces captured Kisangani in August 1998. The Lusaka Peace Agreement of July and August 1999 largely stopped movement on the front lines, but fighting continued. After Kabila's assassination in January 2001, his successor, Joseph Kabila, pursued peace, culminating in the Global and All-Inclusive Agreement of December 17, 2002. The war officially ended on July 18, 2003. The war and its aftermath caused an estimated 5.4 million deaths, mostly from disease, malnutrition and war crimes, making it the deadliest conflict since [[World War II]], according to a 2008 International Rescue Committee report.

Period of rapid scientific discovery, standardization, mass production and industrialization, generally dated 1870–1914 and ending with the start of [[World War I]]. Also called the Technological Revolution, it built on earlier advances such as [[Interchangeable parts|interchangeable parts]] and the Bessemer process for making [[Steel|steel]]. Its main developments included [[Electricity|electrical power]], the [[Telephone|telephone]], petroleum, the [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engine]] and synthetic chemicals such as dyes and fertilizers. Railroads and cheap steel reinforced each other, and the United States laid 75,000 miles of track in the 1880s, the largest amount in world history. Railroad and telegraph expansion allowed unprecedented movement of people and ideas, feeding a new wave of [[Colonialism|colonialism]] and [[Globalization|globalization]]. David Landes's 1966 essay and his 1972 book *The Unbound Prometheus* standardized scholarly use of the term.

Palestinian uprising against [[Israel]] and its occupation, 2000–2005, also known as the Al-Aqsa Intifada. It began with civilian protests by Arab residents of East Jerusalem and areas within Israel proper, then escalated into violence in Israel, the [[West Bank]] and the [[Gaza Strip]]. Violence increased from September 2000, after [[Ariel Sharon]] visited the [[Temple Mount]], and Israeli police responded with rubber bullets, live ammunition and tear gas. After March 2001, Palestinian militant groups carried out about 138 suicide bombings, mostly targeting Israeli civilians. About 1,000 Israelis were killed. The uprising ended with the Sharm el-Sheikh Summit of 2005, when Mahmoud Abbas and Sharon agreed to de-escalate.

War of aggression waged by Italy against Ethiopia from October 1935 to May 1936, regarded as the largest colonial campaign in history. Italian forces attacked from Eritrea and Somalia on October 3, 1935, without a declaration of war, and captured [[Addis Ababa]] on May 5, 1936. [[Benito Mussolini]] replaced General Emilio De Bono with Pietro Badoglio in November 1935. Italian aircraft dropped mustard gas, in violation of the 1925 Geneva Protocol. Emperor [[Haile Selassie]] fled into exile on May 2, 1936, and Mussolini announced the annexation of Ethiopia on May 9, forming Italian East Africa. The war ended Italy's Stresa Front alliance with the Western powers and led to rapprochement with [[Nazi Germany]]. The [[League of Nations]] could not prevent the invasion, which discredited it. Hundreds of thousands of Ethiopian civilians died, which some historians describe as [[Genocide|genocide]].

War between the United Kingdom and France and the [[Qing dynasty]] of China, 1856–1860, also called the Second Anglo-Chinese War or Arrow War. It followed the [[First Opium War]] and ended in a second Qing defeat and the forced legalization of the [[Opium|opium]] trade. The war began on October 8, 1856, when Qing officials seized the *Arrow*, a British-registered ship. British and French forces captured [[Guangzhou]] (Canton) in December 1857, then took the Taku Forts and stormed [[Tianjin]] in May 1858. The Xianfeng Emperor refused to ratify the Treaty of Tientsin, and fighting resumed. Allied forces occupied [[Beijing]] in 1860, and Lord Elgin ordered the Old Summer Palace looted and burned. The Convention of Peking, signed October 24, 1860, ceded the Kowloon Peninsula to Britain as part of [[Hong Kong]]. Treaties with Russia ceded more than 1.5 million square kilometers (0.58 million square miles) in the north-east and north-west.

Conflict between the Republic of China and the [[Empire of Japan]] and its puppet states, 1937–1945, often regarded as the start of [[World War II]] in Asia. Japan's 1931 invasion of Manchuria established the puppet state of Manchukuo. Full-scale war began on July 7, 1937, after the Marco Polo Bridge incident near Beijing. Japanese forces captured [[Nanjing]] that year and carried out the Nanjing Massacre, and the Nationalist government relocated to [[Chongqing]]. The Nationalists under [[Chiang Kai-shek]] and the [[Chinese Communist Party]] had fought since 1927 but formed a United Front in 1936. The war reached a stalemate by 1939 and became part of the wider Allied war after Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941. Japan surrendered on September 2, 1945, after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria. The war caused around 20 million deaths, mostly of Chinese civilians.

Twenty-first and most recent ecumenical council of the [[Catholic Church]], held in four sessions at St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City from October 11, 1962, to December 8, 1965. [[Pope John XXIII]] convoked it, and Pope Paul VI presided over its final three sessions and promulgated its sixteen documents. Nearly 2,500 bishops and heads of male religious orders attended at some point. The council approved four constitutions, nine decrees and three declarations on the liturgy, revelation, ecumenism and religious freedom. Its decisions permitted vernacular languages in a liturgy long celebrated almost entirely in Latin. Its meaning remains debated, with some treating it as a body of texts and others as a historical event worked out in later decades.

[[International System of Units|SI]] base unit of time, symbol s. It was originally defined as 1/86,400 of a day, since the day divides into 24 hours, 60 minutes and 60 seconds. That Earth-rotation definition is still used by the UT1 system. The current SI definition fixes the frequency of the ground-state hyperfine transition of the [[Caesium|cesium]]-133 atom at 9,192,631,770 [[Hertz|hertz]], equal to s⁻¹. The cesium-based definition was adopted in 1967, and a [[Leap second|leap second]] was added at irregular intervals to civil time between 1972 and 2016 to keep clocks in step with [[Earth's rotation|Earth's rotation]]. The first timekeepers able to count seconds accurately were 17th-century [[Pendulum|pendulum]] clocks. Prefixes form milliseconds, microseconds and nanoseconds, and a 1-gigahertz microprocessor has a cycle time of 1 nanosecond.

Physical law based on empirical observation that heat always flows spontaneously from hotter to colder regions. It establishes [[Entropy|entropy]] as a physical property of a thermodynamic system, and the entropy of an isolated system left to spontaneous evolution cannot decrease. The law forbids what the [[First law of thermodynamics|first law]] would allow, such as a broken cup reassembling and jumping back onto a table. Sadi Carnot showed in 1824 that the efficiency of a heat engine has an upper limit. Rudolf Clausius gave the first rigorous entropy-based definition in the 1850s. [[Statistical mechanics]] explains the law through probability distributions of large assemblies of atoms or molecules.

Stage of formal education that follows [[Primary education|primary education]] and precedes higher education, usually for students aged 12 to 18. Lower secondary education is the final phase of basic education, and upper secondary education is the phase immediately before [[Tertiary education|tertiary education]]. In most countries it is compulsory at least until age 16. Since 1989, Article 28 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child has stated that secondary education, general and vocational, should be available and accessible to every child. In medieval times the church provided it for the sons of nobility and for boys preparing for universities and the priesthood. After the [[Reformation]], the state took control of learning, and [[John Locke|John Locke]] and Comenius shifted teaching toward building knowledge. The right to secondary education was codified after 1945.

Organization whose activities, membership, inner functioning and sometimes existence are concealed from outsiders. The term usually excludes covert groups such as intelligence agencies or guerrilla insurgencies, which hide their activities but maintain a public presence. Definitions generally rely on the degree of secrecy, the transmission of secret knowledge, denial of membership, personal bonds among members, and secret rites. Historian Richard B. Spence defines a secret society as a group whose existence is usually public but whose beliefs or practices are concealed behind an oath, promising members superior status or knowledge. Historian Jasper Ridley called [[Freemasonry]] "the world's most powerful secret Society." [[Italy]] and [[Poland]] ban secret political parties in their constitutions. Many undergraduate societies at American universities, such as Skull and Bones at [[Yale University]], have been considered secret societies.

American [[Thoroughbred|Thoroughbred racehorse]], nicknamed Big Red, and ninth winner of the American Triple Crown, in 1973. He was the first Triple Crown winner in 25 years and set speed records in all three races, including a 31-length victory in the Belmont Stakes that is often considered the greatest race ever run by a thoroughbred. He won five Eclipse Awards and Horse of the Year honors at ages two and three. Syndicated for a record $6.08 million, he became the leading broodmare sire in North America in 1992 through his daughters' offspring. He died of laminitis in 1989 at age 19.

sort_key: secretary general of the united nations
entry: De facto head of the United Nations, who oversees the UN Secretariat, one of the six principal organs. The secretary-general acts as the Security Council's executive officer, overseeing implementation of its decisions and mandates. The General Assembly appoints the secretary-general on the recommendation of the Security Council, where any of the five permanent members can veto a nomination. Chapter XV of the UN Charter (Articles 97 to 101) sets out the role, while qualifications and tenure rest on custom. Appointees have all been career diplomats, usually serving five-year terms. Since 1981 the Security Council has voted in secret straw polls, and no candidate has ever been rejected by the General Assembly.

Large terrestrial [[Bird of prey|bird of prey]] (*Sagittarius serpentarius*) endemic to [[Sub-Saharan Africa|sub-Saharan Africa]], placed in its own family, Sagittariidae. It stands as much as 1.3 meters (4 feet 3 inches) tall on crane-like legs, with grey plumage, black flight feathers and thighs, and a flattened dark crest. It is usually found on open grasslands and savanna, where it hunts on foot, stomping prey such as insects and small vertebrates. The nest is built at the top of a thorny [[Acacia|acacia]] tree, and a clutch of one to three eggs is laid. John Frederick Miller described the species in 1779. Habitat destruction has caused a rapid population decline, and the species is classed as endangered. It appears on the coats of arms of South Africa and Sudan.

Subgroup of a religious, political or philosophical belief system, typically an offshoot of a larger organization. From Latin *secta*, "a way" or "road," the term originally referred to religious groups that had separated from a main body. It now applies to any group that diverges to follow distinct beliefs and practices, often from a perception of [[Heresy|heresy]]. [[Max Weber|Max Weber]] and Ernst Troeltsch were among the first to define sects within the church-sect typology, as voluntary associations whose membership comes from personal acceptance of doctrine rather than birth. Sects usually are more radical and ethically strict than mainstream churches. Roy Wallis described sects by "epistemological authoritarianism," whereas [[Cult|cults]] are marked by "epistemological individualism."

Protection from, or resilience against, potential harm or unwanted coercion. Beneficiaries of security may be persons, social groups, objects, institutions or ecosystems. The term also describes the absence of harm, the presence of an essential good (food security), secrecy (a secure telephone line) and containment (a secure cell). Security is both a feeling and a state of reality, so a person may feel secure without being safe, or insecure despite being safe. Protective measures include locks, fences, walls, [[Armour|armor]] and antivirus software, along with warning systems such as alarms and [[Radar|radar]]. Coercive capabilities include [[Aircraft carrier|aircraft carriers]], [[Handgun|handguns]] and [[Firearm|firearms]]. Approaches are contested: some argue that security depends on protective and coercive power, others on equitable relationships and meeting fundamental needs.

[[Car|Passenger car]] in a three-box configuration, with separate compartments for the engine, passengers and cargo; known as a saloon in British English. Typical features include a B-pillar supporting the roof, two rows of seats, and a less steeply sloping roofline than a coupé, giving rear passengers more headroom. The name derives from the 17th-century sedan chair, an enclosed box carried by porters. The first recorded use of the term for an automobile body style was in 1912. Sedans became the dominant passenger car style in the United States and Europe by the mid-20th century, but their market share has declined since the late 1990s as sport utility vehicles and crossovers have gained favor.

Loose solid particles transported and deposited on a planetary surface by water, wind, ice or gravity. Sediment forms through [[Weathering|weathering]] and [[Erosion|erosion]] of existing rocks. Sand and silt carried in river water settle on the seabed, and if buried, they may become [[Sandstone|sandstone]] and siltstone through lithification. Most sediment is moved by water, but wind forms desert dunes and loess, and glaciers deposit moraine and till. Grain size is measured on the log base 2 Phi scale, from colloid to boulder. Shape is described by form, roundness and surface texture, and composition by parent rock, mineral makeup and chemistry. Stronger flows lift and drag particles more, while larger or denser particles are more likely to fall through the flow.

Region-scale depression of Earth's crust in which long-term subsidence allows a thick sequence of [[Sediment|sediment]] to accumulate and become [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary rock]]. Basins form when deformation of the lithosphere, usually linked to plate tectonics, creates space for sediment. Mechanisms include thinning of the crust, loading by sediment or volcanic and tectonic forces, and changes in the density of the underlying lithosphere. Once formed, the weight of accumulating sediment accentuates subsidence. More than 600 basins have been identified worldwide, ranging from tens of square kilometers to over a million, with sedimentary fills from 1 to almost 20 kilometers thick. Almost all the world's [[Natural gas|natural gas]], [[Petroleum|petroleum]] and [[Coal|coal]] is found in sedimentary rock, making basins economically important.

Rock formed by the cementation of [[Sediment|sediment]], particles of mineral or organic matter that accumulate at Earth's surface. Sedimentation may also occur when dissolved minerals precipitate from water. Sedimentary rocks cover much of the continents but make up a small share of the crust's volume, forming a thin veneer over igneous and metamorphic rock. They are deposited in layers called strata and are often found in large [[Sedimentary basin|sedimentary basins]]. Clastic rocks are made of cemented fragments such as [[Conglomerate (geology)|conglomerate]] and [[Sandstone|sandstone]], while biochemical and chemical rocks include [[Limestone|limestone]] and coal. Their layers preserve evidence of Earth's history, including paleoclimate and the history of life, and they are sources of fossil fuels, drinking water and ores.

[[Dwarf planet|Dwarf planet]] in the outermost Solar System, orbiting the Sun far beyond [[Neptune]]. It is roughly 1,000 km in diameter, and its surface is a mixture of ices of water, carbon dioxide and ethane, with reddish tholins. It is not expected to have a substantial atmosphere, and it is tied with Ceres as the largest dwarf planet not known to have a moon. Sedna takes about 11,400 years to orbit the Sun, on one of the widest and most elliptical orbits known. Its orbit may have been perturbed by a close encounter with the hypothetical [[Planet Nine|Planet Nine]]. Michael Brown, Chad Trujillo and David Rabinowitz discovered it on November 14, 2003.

Japanese video game company and subsidiary of Sega Sammy Holdings, headquartered in [[Tokyo]]. Founded as Nihon Goraku Bussan by Martin Bromley and Richard Stewart on June 3, 1960, it became Sega Enterprises in 1965 after acquiring an importer of coin-operated games. Sega produced arcade games and developed its own consoles from 1983 until 2001, after which it became a third-party developer and publisher. Its franchises include [[Sonic the Hedgehog]], Total War, Virtua Fighter and Persona. Sammy Corporation acquired Sega in 2004, and in 2020 Sega Games and Sega Interactive merged into Sega Corporation.

16-bit home video game console developed by [[Sega]], known as the Mega Drive outside North America. It was released in Japan as the Mega Drive in October 1988 and in North America as the Genesis in August 1989. It was adapted from Sega's System 16 arcade board, and its library exceeded 800 games. Success in North America, Brazil, Australia and Europe was helped by [[Sonic the Hedgehog]], released in 1991. The console sold 30.75 million units worldwide. Add-ons such as the Sega CD and 32X were unsuccessful, and the console was succeeded by the [[Sega Saturn]] in 1994.
